textClass.keywords: Tumor-on-a-chip (TOC) Microfluidics CAR T cells Cancer immunotherapy T cell engineering IL13Rα2

div.p: Immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells have shown promising outcomes in hematological cancer but face challenges in targeting solid tumors like glioblastoma (GBM). Advancing this therapy for GBM has been hindered by the lack of preclinical tools that accurately model the complex interplay between CAR T cells and tumor cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME) -interactions critical for optimizing CAR constructs and improving efficacy. Physiologically relevant models that closely mimic the solid TME are therefore highly sought after in developing CAR T therapies. Here, we report a microengineered glioblastoma-ona-chip (GOC) model with a functional vascular network to investigate the efficacy and selectivity of IL-13 mutein CAR T cells (TV-13) against U87 GBM tumor cells expressing high interleukin-13 receptor alpha-2 (IL13Rα2), compared with the ubiquitously expressed IL13Rα1. This biomimetic platform recapitulates the GBM TME and enables dynamic evaluation of CAR T cell responses under locoregional administration, paralleling clinical approaches. Using the organotypic GOC model, we evaluated CAR T cell-mediated inhibition of GBM invasion, monitored real-time dynamic CAR T-U87 interactions, and quantified the release of cytotoxic, proinflammatory, and stimulation-associated cytokines as measures of T cell effector function. CAR T cells induced a densitydependent reduction in U87 migration, accompanied by robust cytokine release, while TV-13 maintained specificity towards IL13Rα2 tumor antigen over IL13Rα1. Additionally, we further demonstrated the efficacy of CAR T cells against patient-derived GBM cells within the GOC model. Collectively, these findings highlight the GOC platform as a powerful preclinical screening tool for cancer immunotherapy optimization.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common, aggressive, and malignant primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by a poor prognosis [1][2][3]. Standard treatment regimens include maximal surgical resection followed by concurrent daily chemotherapy and radiotherapy [4]. Unfortunately, these procedures extend median survival to only about 14 months, highlighting the urgent need for more effective treatments [5]. In this context, cancer immunotherapy that precisely modulates the immune cells to target the cancer cells remains a crucial area of ongoing investigation.

Among the various immunotherapeutic strategies, adoptive T cell therapy, particularly chimeric antigen receptor-modified T (CAR T) cell therapy, involves genetically engineering a patient's T cells to express synthetic receptors (CARs) that selectively bind tumor-specific antigens and induce targeted tumor cell killing [6][7][8][9][10]. Particularly, the success of CAR T cells in treating hematological malignancies has motivated the investigation of this approach for solid tumors [11][12][13][14]. However, despite these advances, applying CAR T therapy to solid tumors like GBM remains largely ineffective due to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), antigen heterogeneity, limited T cell trafficking, and poor T cell persistence [15][16][17]. Consequently, there are currently no FDA-approved CAR-T cell therapies for GBM. To overcome these challenges, efforts should focus on three key strategies: (i) engineering improved CAR T cell products that are both safe and effective against GBM tumors; (ii) optimizing the mode of CAR T administration to overcome physical barriers; and (iii) evaluating these products using a physiologically relevant model systems that more accurately recapitulate the diverse attributes of the solid TME. In this context, interleukin-13 receptor alpha-2 (IL13Rα2) has emerged as a promising biomarker for both the diagnosis and treatment of GBM due to its tumor-restricted overexpression and high-affinity binding to the proinflammatory cytokine IL-13 [18][19][20]. IL13Rα2 is overexpressed in approximately 75 % of GBM samples, making it an attractive target for cancer therapy [21,22]. However, its low-affinity binding partner, IL13Rα1/IL4Rα, is ubiquitously expressed in healthy tissue, posing risks of off-target toxicities for IL13Rα2-targeted therapeutics [23][24][25][26]. To address this, several groups have explored strategies to exploit the tumor-specific expression of IL13Rα2 while preventing heterodimer binding by introducing mutations into IL-13 [18,23,27]. Nguyen et al. engineered a novel quadruple-mutant IL-13 derivative by introducing point mutations at the 13th, 66th, 69th, and 105th amino acids (E13K, R66D, S69D, and K105R) [18]. This novel mutein preferentially bound IL13Rα2-positive tumors at a 7:1 tumor-to-muscle ratio in vivo [18]. Kim and colleagues later developed a CAR incorporating this mutein to deliver clickable nanoparticles across the blood-brain barrier (BBB). They observed trafficking and intratumoral penetration of these first-generation IL-13 mutein (tetravariant-13 or TV-13)-based CAR T cells into the GBM mass in nude mice 24 h post-administration [23]. However, a clear understanding of the interactions between TV-13 CAR and unmodified IL-13 CAR T cells against GBM tumor cells within the TME remains elusive, warranting further investigation.

In addition to optimizing CAR design and architecture, it is crucial to focus on delivery strategies that can overcome the limitations of inefficient CAR T cell trafficking. Accordingly, current clinical trials of CAR T therapy for GBM have focused on locoregional administration, in which CAR T cells are delivered directly into the tumor or adjacent regions [28][29][30]. For instance, an early-phase I clinical trial of anti-IL13Rα2 CAR T cells for GBM demonstrated that locoregional administration improved T cell persistence and tumor control, supporting the rationale for local delivery [31]. However, due to the paucity of clinical data and the lack of standardization in clinical trials, it is difficult to determine the optimal delivery technique for newly developed CAR T cell therapies. To determine the optimal route of administration for CAR T cells in solid tumors, comprehensive preclinical and clinical studies must be conducted to evaluate tumor accessibility, CAR T cell trafficking, therapeutic efficacy, and safety across various delivery methods.

To address these limitations in CAR T development and testing, there is a crucial need for models that better recapitulate the processes of the solid TME and deliver human-relevant results. However, preclinical evaluations are largely focused on conventional 2D in vitro and in vivo models. While 2D in vitro assays are useful for rapidly assessing effector responses, they rely on endpoint analyses and lack critical biological features such as the extracellular matrix (ECM), spatial organization, and vasculature [32]. Thus, with simplified 2D-based assays, replicating the complex cancer immune interactions is unattainable. On the other hand, in vivo animal models are highly sought after to study CAR T interactions, as they reflect system-level complexity [32][33][34]. Although essential for preclinical testing, they possess inherent functional and dimensional limitations, along with high costs, low throughput, and species-specific immune differences that fail to accurately recapitulate the human immune and immune-tumor responses [33,35,36]. These constraints raise concerns about the predictive capacity and significantly reduce the translational value of current in vitro and in vivo models for the development and efficient screening of new CAR T therapies for GBM [37,38]. To holistically assess CAR T therapeutics against solid malignancies, there is a critical need for 3D human organotypic models that establish physiologically relevant environments, bridge the gap between in vitro and in vivo models, and enable direct comparisons of CAR T cell products under identical conditions and customizable setups.

Microfluidic tumor models are advanced, miniaturized systems that recapitulate key biophysical and biochemical features of the TME [39][40][41][42][43]. These platforms consist of interconnected and perfusable media channels at the micrometer scale, enabling precise fluid manipulation [44][45][46]. Microfluidic platforms allow the recreation of the target tissue architecture, spatiotemporally controlled flow, and oxygen gradients, while enabling semi-high-throughput screening of immune-targeted therapies with multi-parameter readouts in a short timeframe [47,48]. Additionally, microfluidic systems provide precise control over cellular components and enable real-time observation of cell-cell interactions, surpassing traditional models [49,50]. Due to these unique advantages, microfluidic-based systems have emerged as powerful tools for engineering tumor-on-a-chip models for cancer research, facilitating the study of various aspects of disease progression [51][52][53][54]. For instance, a study by Nagaraju et al. assessed the influence of 3D vasculature on the metastatic behavior of breast cancer cells [55]. Building on this, other studies have leveraged the 3D tumor-on-a-chip platform to mimic the perivascular niche of GBM, enabling in-depth studies that elucidate cellular interactions between glioma stem cells and specific niche components [56,57]. Another study by Ayuso et al. evaluated the role of TME hypoxia on natural killer cells [48]. In a different study by Manoharan et al. developed a microfluidic model of GBM and utilized the model for evaluating the anti-tumor capabilities of biomimetic nanomedicine [58]. Although numerous studies have focused on modeling and understanding tumor biology, the application of such novel systems to assess CAR T cell behavior and efficacy remains limited. For example, Ando et al. investigated the impact of hypoxia on CAR T cell behavior using a microfluidic model [59], while Wan et al. studied CAR T cell infiltration into a breast tumor spheroid within a parallel microfluidic setup [60]. A recent study by Maulana et al. evaluated the efficacy of anti-ROR1 CAR T cells targeting breast cancer and monitored its associated cytokine release dynamics for a duration of 8 days post CAR treatment using a microfluidic platform [61]. Complementing this study, a recent review on immunotherapy biomarkers in brain metastasis highlighted how cytokines and growth factors that shape the TME dynamics are an enabling biomarker for guiding immunotherapeutic strategies [62]. In another effort, Liu et al. reported the development of a biologically inspired model to study the effector function of CAR T cells against mesothelin-positive lung tumor explants [63]. However, to date, very few studies have utilized microfluidic tumor models to assess CAR T cell therapies for GBM. Therefore, microfluidic systems offer a unique and non-conventional approach to evaluating CAR T cell interactions within a physiologically relevant human context.

Recognizing the need and existing knowledge gap in the thorough evaluation of CAR T therapies for GBM, herein, we report the development of a microengineered glioblastoma-on-a-chip (GOC) model with enhanced cytoarchitecture to study CAR T cell dynamics within a 3D organotypic TME. The central objective of this study is to model locoregional CAR T administration and investigate the functional capacity of our engineered CAR T cells (TV-13 and IL-13) in eradicating IL13Rα2 + tumor cells (U87). In the assessment of cytotoxic capability of our CAR T cells, we observed a significant reduction in GBM cell migration and proliferation within the chip's microenvironment. Additionally, a dose-dependent killing trend was observed across both in vitro and microfluidic GOC experiments. To further elucidate the underlying mechanism of CAR T cell-mediated cytotoxicity, we measured cytokine release kinetics. Functional on-chip evaluation of TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells against IL13Rα2 + tumor cells validated the specificity and reduced off-tumor toxicity of the TV-13 CAR T construct. Lastly, to confirm the ability to generate patient-specific GOC and to assess the efficacy of CAR T cells, we further integrated patient-derived GBM cells (GBM12) into our model system, which consistently revealed antigenspecific CAR T cell anti-tumor activity against patient-derived GBM cells. These findings decisively demonstrate the ability of miniaturized assays to contextualize and deepen our understanding of cell-cell interactions between CAR T cells and their targets within a 3D TME, paving the way for more precise optimization of CAR T therapies for GBM and other solid tumors. Notably, our study provides a unique strategy to comprehensively evaluate the CAR T-GBM interactions using functional and cytokine-based assays beyond CAR T trafficking, using a 3D GOC model that not only mimics the TME architecture but also captures the clinically relevant CAR T administration in a controlled setting. By effectively emulating key aspects of CAR T cell behavior within a biomimetic GBM TME, this platform serves as a valuable model for optimizing and refining CAR therapies prior to preclinical studies and clinical trials.

div.head: Microfluidic device features
div.p: The three-layer GOC microfluidic system, utilized in this study, features three distinct hydrogel regions: the central tumor region (red), the middle stromal region (purple), and the outermost vascular region (green), bounded by two flanking media channels (pink) (Fig. 1A). To achieve spatial organization between these regions, each interface was bounded with microposts spaced evenly at 100 μm. Specifically, the tumor-stroma and stroma-vascular interfaces were bordered by hexagonal microposts, whereas the vascular-media interface was bounded by trapezoidal microposts, creating the necessary surface tension to effectively hold hydrogels in place. The side-by-side arrangement of the tumor-stroma-vascular region offers an advantage by enabling dynamic communication between various cells and facilitating biomolecule diffusion from different regions within the device.

div.head: Vector design
div.p: Amino acid sequences specific to IL-13 were obtained from UniProt (Accession number: P35225). TV-13 features a modified IL-13 serving as the antigen-binding domain, with amino acid substitutions designed to enhance selectivity for the target protein IL13Rα2 while minimizing binding affinity to IL13Rα1. The modifications in TV-13 involve substituting the 13th, 66th, 69th, and 105th amino acids in wild-type IL-13 with E13K, R66D, S69D, and K105R, respectively (Fig. 1B). TV-13 or IL-13 was inserted into a second-generation CAR cassette containing a CD8α signal peptide, CD8α hinge and transmembrane domains, a 4-1BB costimulatory intracellular signaling domain (ICD), and a CD3ζ activation domain. 4-1BB costimulatory domain was selected as it has been used in FDA-approved CD19 CAR T cell therapies and has been shown to enhance T cell persistence and long-term durability [64,65]. These CAR constructs are herein referred to as TV-13 or IL-13 CAR. An eGFP tag was inserted after the CD3ζ region of the TV-13 CAR to enable detection by flow cytometry (Supplementary Figure S1 A, B).

div.head: Cell culture
div.p: T cell Culture: Isolated T lymphocytes were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Institute medium (RPMI)-1640 enriched with 10 % by volume fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1 % 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid (HEPES), 1 % penicillin-streptomycin, and 1 % GlutaMAX. Cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a 1:1 CD4:CD8 ratio at a density of 1 × 10 6 cells/mL and stimulated using CD3/CD28 Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 11141D) at 1:1 cell-to-bead ratio at 37 • C. 24 h after stimulation, T cells were transduced with 200 μL of lentivirus, and at 48 h, the culture volume was adjusted to 4 mL by media supplementation. Cells were debeaded three days after the initial stimulation, maintained at 0.5 × 10 6 cells/mL, and expanded every other day for a nine-day stimulation cycle.

U87 Culture: The Uppsala 87 (U87) Malignant Glioma cell line (HTB-14, ATCC) performed as the target tumor for this study was cultured in complete media composed of Eagle's minimum essential medium (EMEM) with L-Glutamine, and supplemented with 10 % FBS, 1 % HEPES, and 1 % penicillin-streptomycin. These cells were passaged in correlation to their confluency every 4-5 days using 0.05 % Trypsin disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA, Gibco).

GBM12 Culture: Patient-derived GBM cells (GBM12) used as an ontarget cell to test therapeutic and tumor-specific effects were obtained from Dr. Nhan Tran (Mayo Clinic, Phoenix) and cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle medium (DMEM) media supplemented with 10 % FBS, 1 % penicillin-streptomycin, 1 % GlutaMAX, and 1 % HEPES. The cells were passaged every two to three days when cells reached a confluency of 75-80 % using 0.05 % Trypsin EDTA and were used between passages 3-6.

BEC Culture: Primary Human Brain Microvascular Endothelial Cells (BECs) from Cell Systems (ACBRI 376) were cultured in Cell Systems growth medium supplemented with CultureBoost™. Cells were detached from the flask once they reached a confluency of 80 % using 0.25 % Trypsin EDTA and cultured in a T-75 flask coated with Attachment Factor™. These cells were passaged every 2-3 days and were used in experiments between passages 5-10.

PC Culture: Human brain vascular pericytes (PCs) from ScienCell (#1200) were cultured in pericyte medium (ScienCell #1201) on a polyl-lysine-coated flask. Cells were detached from the flask using 0.25 % Trypsin EDTA and used between passages 3-6.

HT-1080 Culture: Human fibrosarcoma cells (CCL-121, ATCC or HT-1080) were used to generate an off-target cell line (IL13Rα1 + HT-1080) expressing IL13Rα1-T2A-mCherry gene, which was single-sorted for the experiments described here. The cells were cultured in complete media consisting of EMEM with L-Glutamine, and supplemented with 10 % FBS, 1 % HEPES, and 1 % penicillin-streptomycin. These cells were passaged in correlation to their confluency every 2-3 days using 0.25 % Trypsin EDTA.
All cells were cultured in a humidified incubator maintained at 37 • C and 5 % CO 2 and were routinely tested for mycoplasma using a sensitive and reliable method.

div.head: Cell injection into 3D GOC model
div.p: A working solution of fibrin gel was prepared by dissolving Fibrinogen (6 mg/mL) and Thrombin (4 U/mL) separately in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and endothelial cell growth medium-2 microvascular (EGM-2 MV, bullet kit, Lonza) media and kept on ice. To establish the self-assembled microvascular network (μVN), BECs and PCs were detached from the flask, spun down, and resuspended in Thrombin solution at a concentration of 72 × 10 6 cells/mL and 4 × 10 6 cells/mL (master cell stock), respectively, and kept on ice. Master cell stocks were then mixed with Fibrinogen solution in a 1:1 ratio to form the fibrin gel. The prepared Fibrin cell mixture was quickly injected into the vascular region of the device and allowed to crosslink for 15 min at room temperature (RT). After cross-linking, devices were cultured in EGM-2 MV media supplemented with 50 ng/mL of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) for 7 days, where the media was exchanged every 24 h (Fig. 1C).

To mimic the clinical administration (locoregional) of CAR T cells within our GOC model, we established a dense tumor core surrounded by a stroma region containing T cells of varying densities (Supplementary Table 1). For tumor and stroma injections, U87 and T cells (UTD [untransduced T cell, control], IL-13, and TV-13) were detached and resuspended in their respective culture medium at the desired concentration based on the culture conditions (Supplementary Table 1). To establish the dense tumor, U87 cells mixed at a 1:1 ratio of Matrigel® (Corning, Basement Membrane Matrix, LDVE-free) were injected into the tumor region and cross-linked at 37 • C for 4 min and flipped every 2 min. Upon cross-linking the tumor region, a 1:1 mixture of T cells and Matrigel® was prepared and carefully injected into the stroma region and cross-linked for 6 min, flipping every 2 min. Finally, the established tissue within the GOC model was cultured in a media cocktail containing a 1:1 ratio of RPMI media (without FBS) and EMEM (Fig. 1C and D). The final concentration of FBS in the media cocktail was maintained at 5 % FBS to match the concentration of media used for 2D assays.

div.head: CAR verification and tumor phenotyping
div.p: To verify the efficacy of the lentiviral transduction, co-cultured T cells were evaluated on day 4 of the stimulation cycle for their viability, CD4 and CD8 expression, and CAR expression using anti-IL13 staining. Cells were quantified, and 0.4 × 10 6 cells were divided evenly between stained and unstained samples. After being washed with Dulbecco's PBS (dPBS), cells were incubated in the dark for 10 min at 4 • C with a 100 μL of viability dye (eFluor780) diluted at 1:2000. The reaction was quenched with 200 μL of fluorescence-activated cell sorting buffer (FACS) (formula: 20 % FBS, 1 mM EDTA, 1 L dPBS) and cells were pelleted by centrifugation. Anti-CD4, CD8, and IL-13 antibodies were added at a 1:100 dilution in a 50 μL staining volume, followed by incubation in the dark for 20 min at 4 • C. Unstained samples were subjected to the same washing steps and incubation times as the stained samples. All cells were then fixed with 2 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 5 min at 4 • C, washed with FACS buffer, and resuspended in a final volume of 200 μL FACS buffer for flow cytometric analysis. In addition, the TV-13 CAR construct contained an eGFP reporter gene, which served as a marker of CAR transduction and was analyzed by flow cytometry (Supplementay Fig. S1 A, B).

U87, HT-1080, and GBM12 cells were phenotyped across passages 3-18, 3-10, and 3-6, respectively, for IL13Rα2 and IL13Rα1 expression using anti-IL13Rα2 and anti-IL13Rα1 antibodies, following the staining protocol described above for CARs. Samples were analyzed by flow cytometry.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Statistical Analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 10.6.0 software. Unless mentioned, all graphs are represented as mean ± SD. For the microfluidic GOC model, data were collected from three independent experiments with at least four technical replicates for the invasion assay and with at least two technical replicates for the IF staining experiments. For cytokine analysis, effluents were pooled from three independent experiments with six to eight technical replicates. Furthermore, the 2D flow cytometry data shown are from representative donors. Our Simplified Presentation of Incredibly Complex Evaluations (SPICE) analysis was completed using FlowJo by creating Boolean gates of marker-positive subpopulations to identify cells expressing simultaneous or single cytokines during coculture. Further details on the statistical analysis, donor information, and biological replicates are provided in the respective figure legends.

div.head: Assessment of CAR transduction efficiency and IL13Rα2 expression on U87 cells
div.p: Prior to the addition of the CAR T cells into the 3D GOC model, the T cells were prepared and assessed for efficient CAR transduction to reflect their therapeutic potential against IL13Rα2-expressing GBM cells (Fig. 2A). Primary human T cells isolated from healthy donors were activated and transduced with lentiviral plasmids encoding IL-13 and TV-13 CARs, each containing 4-1BB costimulatory domains. In contrast to the earlier study [23], the TV-13 CAR evaluated here is implemented within a second-generation CAR framework. Both the TV-13 CAR and the unmodified IL-13 CAR examined in this study share an identical second-generation backbone, including the same 4-1BB costimulatory domain, enabling a controlled comparison that isolates the contribution of the TV-13 binding domain independent of CAR signaling architecture.

Transduction efficiency was assessed on day 4 of their stimulation cycle. CAR expression on the T cell surface was determined by flow cytometry using anti-IL13 Phycoerythrin (PE), following a gating strategy that included differentiating lymphocytes, selecting live singlets, distinguishing CD4 and CD8 populations, and finally identifying CAR expression via IL-13 (Fig. 2B). Compared to the UTD T group (Control), which showed no CAR expression, IL-13 CAR had an average expression of 96.7 % across all donors, and TV-13 averaged 70.6 % (Fig. 2C). Due to the amino acid substitutions introduced into IL-13 during the design of the TV-13, anti-IL-13 PE staining may not fully capture the presence of CAR molecules on the surface of TV-13 CAR T cells. Therefore, we also assessed the TV-13 CAR transduction efficiency by linking the CAR gene to eGFP via a self-cleaving T2A peptide and measuring eGFP intensity by flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. S1A, B). A representative flow plot in Fig. 2D shows the expression of the target antigen IL13Rα2 on the U87 cells.

div.head: TV-13 CAR replicates polyfunctional response of IL-13 CAR in 2D in vitro co-culture assay
div.p: After confirming successful transduction of both CAR constructs, we assessed the effector activity of IL-13 and TV-13 in the presence of U87 by quantifying the release of inflammatory cytokines. CAR T therapies have shown their ability to effectively identify tumor-specific antigens and produce cytokines such as TNF-α and IFN-γ, which help direct the immune response toward the target [66]. We aimed to quantify both intracellular and total secreted expression of these cytokines, including IL-2, which promotes T cell survival and persistence, to assess T cell activation, target binding, and the anti-tumor activity of our CARs. Additionally, we measured intracellular levels of perforin and granzyme B, which synergistically coordinate target cell death, to evaluate the killing potential [67]. Each T cell group -UTD, TV-13, and IL-13 -was co-cultured on day 5 of its stimulation cycle at a 1:2 effector to target (E: T or T cell:U87) cell ratio for a total of 5 h and stained for extracellular and intracellular markers (Fig. 3A). Cytokine response was quantified via flow cytometry and followed our standard gating strategy (Fig. 3B). UTD remained inactive with no cytolytic activity, while TV-13 and IL-13 expressed an average of 20.4 % and 25.8 % double-positive TNF-α and IL-2 expression, respectively (Fig. 3C). These findings indicate nearly 20-fold higher cytokine secretion, suggesting that our CARs enhance cytotoxicity and improve proliferative potential compared to UTD when co-cultured with U87 cells (Fig. 3C).

We observed IFN-γ expression of 7.6 % and 11.2 % from TV-13 and IL-13, respectively, compared to 0.65 % from UTD averaged across four biological replicates (Fig. 3D). Perforin and granzyme B displayed a similar trend, highlighting the greater capacity of TV-13 and IL-13 for effector response and cytotoxicity (Fig. 3E). Although UTD expressed an average of 41.5 % granzyme B, potentially arising from basal responses to allogeneic U87 cells, there were no significant levels of perforin to initiate apoptosis in the target cells [68]. We observed a 1.6-and 1.7-fold increase in granzyme B secretion from TV-13 and IL-13, respectively, compared to UTD, along with a similar trend of increased perforin secretion by both CARs compared to UTD (Fig. 3E). Additionally, evaluation of IFN-γ expression in bulk serum revealed increased secretion of this cytokine in the presence of TV-13 and IL-13, compared to UTD T cells (Fig. 3F). Corroborating this, the measurement of the rate of tumor lysis (% cytotoxicity) demonstrated stronger lysis in the presence of TV-13 and IL-13 CARs but not in UTDs, underscoring the superior anti-tumor capabilities of CAR towards target antigen (Fig. 3G).

Beyond using cytokine activity as a measure of CAR T cell potency, we have employed single-cell polyfunctionality analysis via SPICE to assess preclinical CAR T effectiveness (Fig. 3H). This approach enables a comprehensive evaluation of both the benefits and risks of CAR T therapy by capturing multiple functional markers at the single-cell level, providing a more nuanced understanding of its therapeutic potential [69][70][71]. The ability of engineered T cells to secrete more than one cytokine during an immune response has been correlated with high effectiveness, potentiation, and longevity, which translates to improved CAR T cell performance [25,69]. Our flow cytometry results were normalized to the number of CAR-positive T cells measured for their expression of TNF-α, IFN-γ, and IL-2. Our SPICE analysis showed 23.4 % and 29.4 % polyfunctional cells expressing two or more of these cytokines in the TV-13 and IL-13 conditions compared to 0.07 % in the UTD group across all three biological replicates (Fig. 3H). Overall, both CAR constructs initiated polyfunctional immune responses in the presence of U87 cells, which indicates successful targeting, binding, and cytotoxic potential in a 2D mono-culture assay [18].

div.head: Formation of 3D self-assembled microvascular network (μVN)
div.p: To better assess and study the efficacy of CAR T cells against GBM tumors in a physiologically relevant environment, we established an organotypic GOC model that closely mimics the vascular niche of the tumor and surrounding brain tissue. The vascular niche within the model system was established in the third layer of the device by coculturing BECs with PCs at a final density of 19 × 10 6 cells/mL. Fibrin was selected as the matrix for embedding BECs and PCs due to its widespread application in supporting the vasculogenesis process [72]. After the injection of the cell hydrogel mixture, the devices were cultured in EGM-2MV media supplemented with 50 ng/mL VEGF for a total duration of 7 days (Fig. 4A(i-ii)).

Elongation of the ECs and PCs was observed one day after injection, with interconnectivity forming between days 3 and 5 of culture. By the end of seven days, further development of the vascular network, known as the microvascular network (μVN), which features an open lumen and thick vascular bundles, was observed (Fig. 4B and C). Notably, the presence of PCs facilitated better organization of BECs during the selfassembly process by promoting the formation of stable vascular bundles (Fig. 4B). Furthermore, characterization of the established μVN through fluorescent staining for cell-specific markers (CD31: BEC, α-SMA: PC) revealed the localization of pericytes around the vasculature, mimicking the cytoarchitecture of the in vivo vascular niche (Fig. 4B(ii) and 4E). Additionally, co-staining of the μVN with endothelial markers (CD31: green and CD144: red) demonstrated the formation of junctional boundaries in endothelial cells by the end of the culture period (Fig. 4B(i) and Supplementary Video S1). In addition to these, assessment of permeability through FITC Dextran dye and perfusion of microbeads (size: 2 μm) from the media channel through the vascular bundles further confirms the functional capability of the established μVN (Fig. 4D and F, and Supplementary Video S2). These findings highlight the model's improved ability to recapitulate human brain μVN and provide a biomimetic tool to test the efficacy of the proposed CAR T therapy.

div.head: Influence of 3D μVN on GBM cells
div.p: To delineate the influence of vascular components on GBM invasion, we established two different models: (i) mono-culture of U87 (U87 only) and (ii) co-culture of U87 with μVN (U87+μVN). We chose U87 as the model cell type for this study due to its well-established characterization in previous studies [73,74] and higher expression of IL13Rα2 tumor antigen. In the case of U87-only conditions, U87 cells mixed with Matrigel® at a final density of 15 × 10 6 cells/mL were injected into layer 1 (the tumor region) of the microfluidic model, while the other regions remained acellular. Conversely, in the U87+μVN condition, U87 cells mixed with Matrigel® were injected into the device containing established vasculature.

In the tumor model without vasculature (U87-only), U87 cells that migrated into layer 2 (the stromal region) exhibited singular migratory behavior with a strikingly different morphology. In contrast, tumor cells in the U87+μVN condition displayed chain migratory behavior, characterized by a distinctively elongated, needle-like morphology (Fig. 4G (i)). These observations were evident and became more pronounced from day 1 to day 2. Importantly, we observed that vascular integrity was maintained in the presence of U87 cells (U87+μVN), as evidenced by orthogonal sectioning of the μVN (Fig. 4G(ii)). Findings from this preliminary assay underscore the influence of the μVN in attracting U87 cells toward the vascular components, consistent with previous studies [5,75]. Consequently, the U87+μVN condition was used for all downstream screenings.

div.head: Microfluidic characterization of IL-13 mutein CAR T cells against GBM
div.p: To further investigate the differences in T cell effector function in a physiologically relevant context, we compared the UTD and CAR T cells by incorporating them alongside the dense U87 tumor core within our GOC system containing the vasculature (i.e., μVN). We primarily assessed the IL13Rα2-targeting ability of TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells by evaluating the migratory behavior of tumor cells using the microfluidic GOC invasion assay. For the characterization of GOC invasion, we tested four different E:T ratios, namely (i) 0.3:1, (ii) 0.4:1, (iii) 0.5:1, and (iv) 1:1 (Fig. 5A(i)).

After 7 days of μVN network establishment, both U87 cells and T cells (UTD, IL-13, and TV-13) were introduced into the tumor and stroma regions of the GOC device, respectively (Fig. 5A(ii)). This setup, with T cells cultured in the stroma region and U87 in the tumor core while bypassing the μVN, effectively recapitulates the localized delivery of T cells observed in locoregional administration currently being evaluated in clinical trials. We employed a two-fold approach to evaluate the efficacy and lytic capacity of T cells against IL13Rα2-expressing U87 cells. First, we assessed the T cells under four different concentrations -4,6, 8, and 15 × 10 6 T cells/mL-while maintaining the U87 cell concentration at a constant of 15 × 10 6 cells/mL. Particularly, T cell densities of 4,6, 8, and 15 × 10 6 cells/mL correspond to E:T cell ratios of (i) 0.3:1, (ii) 0.4:1, (iii) 0.5:1, and (iv) 1:1, respectively. Second, we monitored and measured the migratory potential of the U87 cells as a functional readout to evaluate the efficacy of the incorporated T cells to control tumor progression. Cells were cultured within the model system for 72 h, and the reduction in migration was quantified by measuring the migration distance (Fig. 5A(iii)).

Varying T cell concentrations revealed a density-dependent effect on tumor cell growth (Fig. 5B(i)). Notably, CAR T cells at lower densities (4 × 10 6 /mL) resulted in a similar U87 cell migration distance as UTD T cells across all donors (Fig. 5B(i)). In contrast, CAR T cells (TV-13 and IL-13) at higher densities (6, 8, and 15 × 10 6 cells/mL) significantly restricted the U87 migration compared to UTD T cells, indicating their effector function (Fig. 5B(i)). Both CAR T cell types exhibited comparable cytolytic activity, effectively limiting U87 migration distance at higher densities (Fig. 5B(ii)). Furthermore, the reduced number of active U87 cells (green) in the stroma region, particularly at higher CAR T densities, further underscored their potency (Fig. 5B). In contrast, UTD T cells allowed U87 cells to migrate into the stroma region across all densities with a distinct chain migratory pattern. These findings demonstrate that within a brain-mimetic environment, CAR T cells (TV-13 and IL-13) not only induce cytotoxicity but also suppress the migratory potential of U87 cells expressing high levels of tumor antigen.

div.head: Real-time impedance-based analysis of the cytotoxic function of CAR T cells
div.p: To further corroborate the cytolytic potential and dose-dependent killing of our CAR T cells, we utilized the xCELLigence Real-Time Cell Analysis MP system to quantify U87 cell death during co-culture with each T cell group. UTD, TV-13, and IL-13 CAR T cells were co-cultured in duplicate with U87 cells on day 6 of their stimulation cycle at E:T ratios of 10:1, 5:1, 2.5:1, 1.25:1, and 0.5:1, and maintained in the platform for 7 days. We observed a significant difference in the normalized cell index for UTD, IL-13, and TV-13 at the 10:1 E:T ratio. Time-course analysis of the average cell index (n = 3 donors) for UTD, TV-13, and IL-13 CAR T cell groups under a 10:1 E:T condition over a 7-day co-culture showed that the UTD cells did not reduce the impedance (or cell index) of the U87 cells (Fig. 5C(i-ii) and Supplementary Fig. S1C(i-iii)), consistent with their lack of cytokine release in the intracellular cytokine assay results. The endpoint cell indices on day 7 clearly show that TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells induced significantly higher U87 cell killing (****p < 0.0001, ***p < 0.001, respectively) compared to the UTD T cells (Fig. 5C (ii)). We also co-cultured each T cell type at E:T ratios that reflect dosedependent CAR T response during treatment. TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells both exhibited a trend of dose-dependent killing within the xCEL-Ligence platform (Fig. 5C(iii-iv) and Supplementary Fig. S1D(i-ii)). Additionally, we measured the percentage of cytolysis with both TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells. Both groups achieved full target cell death, with IL-13 CAR T cells reaching 50 % cytolysis by 34 h of co-culture and TV-13 averaging 66 h (Supplementary Fig. S1E). IL-13 CAR T cells reached 100 % cytolysis by 38 h, while TV-13 reached 99.5 % by 93 h.

div.head: Real-time assessment of motility of GBM and CAR T cells
div.p: Expanding on the observations from the xCELLigence data, we monitored the dynamic interactions between T cells (at the density of 15 × 10 6 cells/mL) and U87 cells within the GOC model using live-cell imaging. To effectively study cellular kinetics, we captured the interactions in real-time over 16 h using time-lapse imaging (Fig. 6A(i), Supplementary Videos S3-S8). Furthermore, cancer cells and T cells were analyzed for key migration metrics, including invasion rate, speed, and directionality (Fig. 6).

Monitoring the tumor cell movement over time through trajectory plots revealed clear differences in the presence of CAR T cells compared to UTD T cells. In the UTD condition, U87 cells exhibited longer trajectories, indicative of directional and active migration (Fig. 6A(ii)). In contrast, in the presence of CAR T cell conditions (TV-13 and IL-13), the trajectories were shorter and less directed, suggesting that CAR T cells not only kill the tumor cells but also actively inhibit their migratory potential, complementing the findings from the invasion assay (Fig. 6A (ii)). To further corroborate this observation, a quantitative assessment of cancer cell invasion rates revealed a reduced invasion rate of U87 cells in the presence of TV-13 and IL-13 T cells compared to UTD cells (Fig. 6A (iii)). Corroborating this, we observed reduced directionality of tumor cells in the presence of CAR T cells compared to the UTD condition (Fig. 6A(iii)). However, an additional evaluation of U87 cells showed comparable tumor cell speeds across different T cell groups (Fig. 6A (iii)). These real-time assessments of U87 cells highlight significant changes in cancer cell dynamics and behavior in response to both CAR T cells and UTD T cells (Fig. 6A).

We also assessed the kinetics of T cells within our model in the presence of target tumor cells (Fig. 6B(i)). Tracking of T cells over time using trajectory plots revealed their motility patterns. Specifically, UTD cells exhibited confined and clustered movement, indicative of reduced motility. On the other hand, CAR T cells displayed more dispersed movement, suggesting increased motility (Fig. 6B(ii)). Furthermore, quantification of the T cell motility revealed that CAR T cells (TV-13 and IL-13) had a higher speed than UTD cells; however, no statistical difference was observed (Fig. 6B(iii)). Assessment of T cell directionality showed a statistically significant increase in directionality for TV-13 and IL-13 T cells, emphasizing the CAR T cells' ability to move toward target tumor cells (Fig. 6B(iii)). Furthermore, we also observed that CAR T cells had a higher speed (although not significant) compared to the UTD T cells, revealing the ability of the engineered T cells to actively migrate within a solid TME (Fig. 6B(iii)). Together, these real-time assessments demonstrated the superiority of engineered T cells in effectively navigating a solid TME and their impact on GBM behavior.

div.head: Alterations in U87 phenotypic behavior and functional immune engagement of T cells
div.p: Based on the 3D invasion assay and real-time migration measurements of both cancer and T cells, we observed a noticeable difference in the morphology and migratory potential of U87 cells. These differences were particularly pronounced at higher T cell densities (15 × 10 6 cells/ mL). Therefore, to further quantitatively assess the density of migrating cells in response to different T cell populations, we measured the number of cells within a field of view (FOV) of the GOC and the number of GBM cells forming a chain during the invasion process. Specifically, we divided the stroma region into two distinct areas, namely near and far areas (Supplementary Fig. S2), and stained the samples for the actin cytoskeleton to assess these specific phenotypic metrics (Fig. 7A). At the same time, CAR T cells have the capability to tip the balance between tumor cell migration and proliferation [76]. To decipher the impact of CAR T cells on tumor growth, in parallel, we further stained the samples for proliferative marker Ki-67 (Fig. 7B).

In addition to evaluating tumor cells, we also measured the engagement of T cells with tumor cells by examining the immune synapse (IS) formation through actin staining. T cells are activated when the CAR's antigen-binding domain recognizes and binds to the target antigen, resulting in the formation of IS, a stable junction (i.e., IS) between E: T cells that is central for CAR T-mediated tumor killing [77]. Thus, to evaluate the IS between CAR T and tumor cells within our model, we assessed the actin reorganization. Notably, we observed numerous T cells in proximity to the tumor (GFP + ) cells. However, in the presence of TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells, T cells were observed to be closely anchored to the tumor cells with a pronounced accumulation of actin at the tumor-CAR T interface, confirming the IS formation (Fig. 7A (i)). Importantly, we frequently observed two to three CAR T cells simultaneously engaging with tumor cells, consistent with active cytotoxic elimination. In contrast, in the presence of UTD, though T cells were present alongside tumor cells, we did not observe any active synapse formation (Fig. 7A(i)). Consistent with these observations, line-scan intensity profiling revealed enrichment of actin at the synaptic interface in the CAR T-treated conditions, underscoring the IS-associated cytoskeletal reorganization. Conversely, in the presence of UTD T cells, the actin fluorescence intensity plot remained distinct, indicating the absence of synapse formation.

Next, tumor cells in the presence of UTD T cells exhibited an increased number of nuclei per chain (Fig. 7A(ii)) and a higher cell count within the FOV (Fig. 7A(iii)), confirming the chain migratory behavior observed from the invasion assay and live imaging. Intriguingly, we did not observe significant differences between the near and far areas, further confirming that UTD T cells had little to no effect on inhibiting the U87 migration. On the contrary, tumor cells in the presence of CAR T cells (both IL-13 and TV-13) showed significantly fewer nuclei per chain as well as fewer cells within the FOV compared to those co-cultured with UTD T cells (Fig. 7A(ii-iii)). Notably, a comparison of cell numbers between near and far areas revealed significantly fewer cells in the far area for both IL-13 and TV-13 CAR T cells, demonstrating the cytolytic capacity of the CAR T cells, which disrupted the chain-like structural organization of U87 cells (Fig. 7A).

Finally, quantification of the Ki-67 index (Ki-67/Nuclei Ratio) showed significantly increased proliferation of U87 cells in the presence of UTD T cells compared to CAR T cells (Fig. 7B(i-ii)). We speculate that the reduced proliferation of U87 cells in the presence of CAR T cells is likely due to the efficacy of the engineered CAR constructs in targeting tumor antigens, thereby initiating a cytotoxic response while simultaneously regulating (i.e., diminishing) tumor cell proliferative capacity. In contrast, UTD T cells, which lack this targeted mechanism, did not inhibit the cancer cell proliferation as effectively as the CAR T cells. These findings underscore the dual role of CAR T cells in controlling GBM progression: by directly eliminating tumor cells and indirectly impairing their metastatic potential by disrupting collective migratory behavior as well as altering (i.e., reducing) tumor cell proliferation.

div.head: Evaluation of cytokine profile in the GOC model using multiplexed microarray analysis
div.p: To further probe into the mechanism of T cell interaction with tumor cells and molecular signaling leading to diminished tumor progression in the case of CAR T cells, we further analyzed cytokine release from CAR T cells in response to U87 cells within our 3D GOC model. Specifically, we utilized the Human CD8/NK Panel LEGENDplex Multi-Analyte Flow Assay Kit to detect proinflammatory, cytotoxic, and stimulatory cytokines (Fig. 8A). Z-score normalized cytokine release, analyzed across varying T cell (E:T) densities, revealed: (i) cytokine production and release occurred exclusively under CAR T cell conditions, with negligible or undetectable levels in UTD T cells, (ii) IL-13 CAR T cells had more effectiveness as compared to TV-13 cells, and (iii) a mostly dose-dependent increase in the release of majority of cytokines, was observed in CAR T (TV-13 and IL-13) conditions (Fig. 8B), with the highest secretion levels measured in 15 × 10 6 T cell density, in majority of cytokines, as compared to the 4 × 10 6 density. These findings highlight the distinct cytokine profile of CAR T cells compared to UTD cells, and the gradual increase in cytokine production indicates a direct relationship between T cell density and effector molecule release.

To further delineate the mechanism of CAR T-mediated tumor killing, we looked into individual cytokine release patterns across varying T cell densities (Fig. 8C and Supplementary Fig. S3). Specifically, we observed excessive production of cytotoxic molecules (Granulysin, Granzyme A, Granzyme B, and Perforin) and stimulatory cytokines (IL-10, TNF-α), along with many other cytokines, in the presence of CAR T cells relative to UTD T cells (Fig. 8C and Supplementary Fig. S3). However, we observed higher release of cytokines associated with cytokine release syndrome (CRS), such as IL-6, TNF-α, INF-γ, even at lower densities of IL-13 T cells, raising potential safety concerns. In contrast, TV-13 cells elicited comparatively lower cytokines associated with CRS, even at higher densities, while maintaining potent antitumor activity, highlighting their effectiveness with reduced safety risks.

Statistical analysis of release kinetics showed the release of many other cytokines such as Fas-L, Fas, and IFN-γ, within our 3D biomimetic GOC (Supplementary Fig. S4). CAR T cells can induce apoptosis in target cells through the death receptor-ligand pairs such as Fas and FasL [77,78]. Findings from our cytokine array revealed increased release of Fas and FasL at higher CAR T cell densities, suggesting the involvement of an additional tumor elimination mechanism (Supplementary Fig. S3 and S4). Together, our cytokine profiling data demonstrated that all the measured cytokines reached peak concentrations at 8 × 10 6 and 15 × 10 6 cells/mL. Furthermore, to move beyond evaluating cytokine changes and to gain insights into how immune activation relates to tumor invasion, we performed a comprehensive correlation analysis (Supplementary Fig. S5). Visualization of the correlation matrix of 13 cytokines and tumor migration distance revealed a strong positive inter-correlation among cytotoxic, pro-inflammatory, and stimulatory cytokines, including IL-2, INF-γ, Granzyme A, Granzyme B, TNF-α, Fas-L, perforin, and granulysin, underscoring a strongly coordinated cytotoxic immune response (Supplementary Fig. S5A(i)). Notably, these cytokines exhibited a consistent negative correlation with tumor migration distance, suggesting an association between heightened immune activation and suppression of tumor invasion. To further validate these network-level observations, we performed Pearson correlation analyses between individual cytokines and tumor migration distance. Increased levels of cytotoxic cytokines such as FasL, Granulysin, and Granzyme B were significantly associated with reduced tumor migration, suggesting an enhanced anti-tumor activity (Supplementary Fig. S5A(ii). Together, these findings demonstrate a strong linkage between immune activation and reduced tumor invasion within our GOC model.

div.head: Effector characterization of TV-13 CAR T cells against IL13Rα1expressing tumor cells
div.p: Imperative to CAR design, antigen specificity is one of the critical aspect, as it governs the ability of CAR T cells to selectively target tumor cells while minimizing off-tumor toxicity. (Fig. 9A). Our 3D microfluidic invasion assay, chain migratory behavior evaluation, and effluent screening revealed the antigen-specific effector function of both CAR T cells (TV-13 and of IL-13). However, to further validate our findings and evaluate the antigen specificity of TV-13 CAR T cells and distinguish their functional response from that of IL-13 CAR T cells, we conducted a 3D invasion assay using tumor only cells expressing IL13Rα1 as a potential off-target antigen. Specifically, we engineered the IL13 receptor family-negative human fibrosarcoma cell line (HT-1080) to overexpress only IL13Rα1 (IL13Rα1 + HT-1080). Successful expression of the antigen on these tumor cells was verified using flow cytometry (Fig. 9B). Next, we evaluated the specificity of TV-13, IL-13, and UTD T cells by coculturing them with IL13Rα1 + HT-1080 cells within our 3D GOC model. Similar to the previous invasion assay, we tested four different E: T ratios as a measure to evaluate the effect of T cell density on tumor growth control (Fig. 9C(i)). Notably, despite the high presence of TV-13 T cells (8 × 10 6 cells/mL and 15 × 10 6 cells/mL), we observed continuous migration of the tumor cells into the stroma region with no observable killing, similar to UTD T cells (Fig. 9C(ii)). On the contrary, in the presence of IL-13 T cells, we observed a density-dependent killing of the tumor cells with a statistically significant difference in tumor killing observed at a higher density of 8 × 10 6 cells/mL 15 × 10 6 cells/ mL T cells, underscoring the off-target toxicity of standard IL-13 CAR T cells (Fig. 9C(ii)). Corroborating this, measurement of chain migratory behavior of the tumor cells that invaded the stroma region clearly showed the increased presence of tumor cells in the presence of TV-13 and UTD T cells as opposed to IL-13 T cells (Fig. 9C(iii)). This clearly demonstrated the superior specificity of TV-13 CAR T cells and functional difference between TV-13 and standard IL-13 CAR T cells. Additionally, this assay demonstrated the utility of our organotypic model in validating the clinically reported off-target effects of CAR T therapy. This result was further supported by the 2D intracellular cytokine release assays. The percentage of IL-13 CAR T cells positive for intracellular IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α at the 1:2 E:T ratio with the IL13Rα1 + HT-1080 cells were significantly higher than those of TV-13 CAR-T cells (p < 0.0001 for both IL-2 and IFN-γ and p < 0.05 for TNF-α) (Fig. 9C(iv)).

div.head: Specificity of CAR T cells against patient-derived GBM cells
div.p: The expression of IL13Rα2 on the tumor cells varies across patients. To capture the heterogeneous expression of the tumor antigen and to show the tumor specificity of the CAR T cells, we additionally incorporated the patient-derived GBM cells (GBM12) into our GOC model. Prior to incorporating into the model, tumor antigen expression was verified by flow cytometry, which confirmed the expression in 76.4 % of GBM12 cells (Fig. 10A). Additionally, 2D evaluation of intracellular cytokine secretions (IFN-γ, IL-2, and TNF-α) and tumor lysis measured by LDH assay revealed the elevated release of cytokine production and increased lytic activity in the presence of CAR Ts compared to UTD controls, confirming the cytotoxic potential of CARs against patientderived tumor cells (Fig. 10B and C). Furthermore, to model a patientspecific microengineered system and to evaluate the CAR T cell antigen specificity within a biologically relevant environment, we integrated the GBM12 cells into our GOC system and evaluated the cytotoxic potential of CAR T cells (Fig. 10D(i) and Supplementary Fig. S6A(i)). Testing the behavior of the tumor cells across the four densities of T cells (UTD, TV-13, and IL-13), we consistently observed effective control of tumor cell migratory potential in the presence of CAR T cells compared to UTD T cells (Fig. 10D(ii)). Notably, we observed the greatest migration of the tumor cells in the presence of UTD T cells. On the contrary, a significant reduction in tumor migration distance in the presence of TV-13 and IL-13 CARs was observed, underscoring the tumor antigenspecific cytotoxicity of the designed CARs (Fig. 10D(ii) and Supplementary Figure S6A(ii)).

Importantly, these patient-derived cells exhibited a unique migratory pattern where we noticed single-cell migration of the tumor cells (green) into the stroma regions (Supplementary Fig. S6B(i, ii)). Evaluation of tumor cells in the stroma region (Near and Far) revealed a clear T-cell dose-dependent reduction in active migrating tumor cells, with a significant reduction in the tumor cells in the presence of 15 × 10 6 /mL of CAR T cells (Fig. 10D(iii)). Furthermore, assessment of actin cytoskeletal reorganization between CAR T (15 × 10 6 /mL) and tumor cells revealed the formation of an immune synapse between tumor cells and T cells (Supplementary Fig. S6C). On the contrary, we did not observe such actin organization in the presence of UTD T cells at a similar density. Together, we show the capability of our GOC model system to capture patient-specificity of CAR T cells.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: CAR T cells have previously demonstrated clinical efficacy against hematological malignancies and are now being explored for the treatment of solid tumors [79]. Insights into solid tumors and the contributions of the evolving TME have fueled the development of advanced CAR therapies with improved efficacy against solid malignancies [80]. In this context, growing research is focused on developing next-generation CARs, such as those targeting IL13Rα2, a tumor-associated antigen overexpressed in GBM and considered a promising target. However, CAR T cells continue to fall prey to the immunosuppressive and structural barriers unique to solid tumors [81,82]. Furthermore, discrepancies between conventional 2D assays and complex 3D models underscore the need for platforms that can accurately assess CAR T cells' interactions in well-controlled experimental settings and environments that better reflect GBM's impact on the TME and immune cell function. Addressing this need, our study integrates engineered T cells into a 3D biomimetic GBM model, providing a significant advancement for investigating CAR T-tumor cell interactions and offering in-depth mechanistic insights that extend beyond those gained from conventional preclinical models.

In recent years, the use of microengineered models has garnered more attention as a system for assessing cancer immunotherapies, including CAR T cells. A recent study utilized a microfluidic model to recapitulate the endothelial-tumor interface to assess the response of CAR T cells against breast cancer. Particularly, this study evaluates the cytokine release during CAR T therapy for 8 days [61]. In a more recent study, the efficacy of CAR T cells for solid tumors (prostate cancer) was evaluated using a tumor-on-a-chip model that modeled the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. They showed that the presence of M2-immunosuppressive macrophages and endothelial cells limits the effector and extravasation of CAR T cells [83]. For instance, a study by Huang et al. utilized a parallel channel BBB-on-a-chip system to visualize the intravasation of CAR T cells towards EGFRvIII + GBM tumor cells [84]. While prior works [23,84] primarily focused on the trafficking of CAR T cells or delivery of TV-13-based CAR T cells, a functional comparison of IL-13 and TV-13 CAR T cells within a vascularized 3D GBM microenvironment has not been reported. Although several emerging studies have investigated adoptive cell therapies, very few studies have utilized this model system to evaluate CAR T interactions in the context of GBM. The studies presented here address this gap by evaluating and contrasting the functional behavior of these CAR T cell products under physiologically relevant tumor conditions that better recapitulate the GBM tumor microenvironment. GBM tumors are highly vascularized structures that create a favorable environment for tumor progression and resistance to therapy [85]. Thus, it is imperative to assess the efficacy of CAR T cells for GBM utilizing a model that mimics vascular-tumor-immune cell interactions. Building on our previous studies that demonstrated the positive impact of vascular niche on GBM invasion [56], we found that the incorporation of μVN enhanced the chain migratory behavior of GBM tumor cells. The presence of μVN may provide growth factors and cytokines that facilitate tumor growth, mimicking the complex environment of solid tumors.

An important finding from the 3D GOC invasion assay was the significantly reduced migratory distance of tumor cells at higher CAR T densities (8 × 10 6 and 15 × 10 6 cells/mL) compared to UTD T cells. Certainly, the observed difference in migratory pattern is primarily attributed to the potent anti-tumor effector functionality of CAR T cells. Upon antigen recognition, CAR T cells form an immune synapse with tumor cells, triggering T cell activation that ultimately leads to the destruction of the tumor cells [86]. We hypothesize that the killing kinetics observed over the 3-day culture period in the GOC model reflect a relatively slower cytotoxic activity of TV-13 compared to IL-13 CAR T cells, indicating a difference in the rate of target cell elimination. Another important aspect of our work is that data from the chain migratory behavior of target cells, alongside the proliferative index of each T cell group, demonstrated that CAR T cells actively mediate cytotoxic killing of both leader and follower cells within migrating chains, collectively resulting in reduced overall tumor progression. A possible explanation for this observation is that disrupting the target cells not only impairs collective tumor cell movement but also significantly reduces tumor growth and progression, potentially through cytokine release by the CAR T cells with potent anti-tumor effects [87]. Additionally, we observed enhanced homing of CAR T cells compared to UTD, with increased directionality during real-time migration, aligning with recent findings [88]. While TV-13 and IL-13 CAR T cells exhibited comparable effects on U87 cell migration, we did not observe enhanced overall killing by TV-13 CAR T cells. However, through on-chip functional characterization of TV-13 and IL-13 CARs against IL13Rα1, we validated the superior specificity of TV-13 CAR T cells towards IL13Rα2 tumor antigen, with significantly reduced off-target toxicity. Additionally, by evaluating the specificity of CARs against GBM12 patient-derived tumor cells, we further demonstrated the translational relevance of our GOC model. Building on this capability, our proposed platform could be extended to assess a range of therapeutic various strategies, such as combinatorial blockade approaches and pharmacological interventions. Moreover, the model provides a unique opportunity to evaluate next-generation CAR designs, such as circulating RNA CARs [89], which hold significant promise for overcoming current limitations of CAR T therapies but remain at an early stage of development. Application of these human-relevant preclinical models could provide valuable insights into the full potential of circulating RNA CARs.

Although functional evaluation showed the dynamic behavior of the CAR T cells, efficacy of the administrated T cells highly relies on their cytokine release mechanism [90]. Results from the multiplexed cytokine array showed that cytokine release was observed within our GOC model only in the presence of CAR T cells, with negligible release in UTD cells. Importantly, we observed a greater release of the majority of cytokines in higher densities of CAR T cells, suggesting a direct correlation between T cell abundance and immune activation. This difference in the cytokine concentration across varying densities is likely driven by the higher number of CAR T cells within the model system, leading to enhanced cytokine release [60]. The observed cytokine profile aligns with the effector functions of CAR T cells, particularly their reliance on IFN-γ and IL-2 to drive cytolytic activity and T cell proliferation [87]. Additionally, the increased release of granzymes (i.e., granzyme B), and perforin highlights the role of CAR T cells in mediating direct tumor cell killing, consistent with prior studies of granule release in CAR T therapy [91,92].

Furthermore, IL-2, an essential cytokine for T cell expansion, exhibited a dose-dependent release, reflecting the CAR T cell activation and proliferation within a 3D environment-both crucial for their sustained antitumor response [93]. Interestingly, IL-6, a key indicator of T cell activation, also demonstrated heightened release in the case of IL-13 CAR T cells, raising concerns regarding cytokine release syndrome (CRS), while the lower IL-6 levels observed with TV-13 suggest a potential safety advantage. Aligning with these findings, we observed a decrease in certain cytokine concentrations in the presence of IL-13 CAR T cells at a density of 15 × 10 6 cells/mL. This reduction, compared to the lower 8 × 10 6 cells/mL condition, could be attributed to enhanced tumor killing at an earlier time point (Day 2) at the higher CAR T cell concentration, and a reduced number of T cell-tumor cell engagements available for cytokine secretion by Day 3, as reported in previous studies [60,61]. Supporting this, our functional assessment from the 3D invasion assay and real-time migration analysis demonstrated reduced tumor growth. However, the continued presence of granzyme B suggests ongoing CAR T-tumor interaction within our model, consistent with previous studies [61]. These results highlight the functional versatility of CAR T cells and the role of cytokine release as a marker of their antitumor efficacy, underscoring the importance of understanding these dynamics for the crucial regulation of therapeutic efficacy with safety. Furthermore, these cytokines released due to cellular interactions could serve as a critical biomarker for guiding the development of precision immunotherapy [62].

Although we observed cytokinetic versatility in our CARs from our SPICE analysis after in vitro co-culture and cytokine array analysis following their culturing period in the 3D GOC model, the vasculature served as an additional metric for assessing safety. We observed preserved vasculature bundles across each dose of UTD T cells, as represented in Supplementary Fig. S7. In contrast, IL-13 CAR T cells caused complete disruption of the vasculature under all the tested densities. Notably, TV-13 CAR T cells maintained some portions of the vasculature at lower densities (4 × 10 6 cells/mL and 6 × 10 6 cells/mL), suggesting their reduced damage on vascular cells at appropriate density. While we did not optimize our doses to determine the balance between effective killing and vasculature damage, we believe that quantifying vasculature integrity serves as a valuable, model-specific benchmark that can guide CAR construct development in the future. Additionally, optimizing the route of CAR T cell administrationfrom intravenous injections to local delivery (i.e. intertumoral) -could help mitigate vasculature damage while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. An important question with the rapid rise in utilizing microfluidic-based models for CAR T evaluation is their ability to generate preclinical accuracy. While our model system provided valuable insights into the dynamics of CAR T efficacy against a solid tumor, it did not entirely mimic the complexities of the immunosuppressive TME, with respect to cellular components. Thus, further studies can use the microfluidic GOC model to comprehensively analyze CAR T cell effectiveness and safety under such conditions by incorporating tumor-associated macrophages, which will pave the way for a better understanding of the challenges encountered by CAR T cells within solid tumors [94,95]. Additionally, although we established a functional μVN with open-lumen structures, we did not assess the perfusion of T cells within our GOC system. In future studies, we will focus on introducing the T cells via perfusion from the media channel into the tumor region through the μVN, enabling the evaluation of the role of the endothelial barriers in T cell trafficking.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this study, we leveraged the modular flexibility of cellular and environmental components to establish a biomimetic GOC system with precise cytoarchitecture, aiming to bridge the current technical and biological knowledge gap in CAR T development for solid tumors. We further expanded our objectives to demonstrate the feasibility of this model for evaluating the efficacy, specificity, and therapeutic function of IL-13 mutein CAR T (TV-13) cells against IL13Rα2 + -expressing GBM tumors, including U87 and patient-derived GBM cells, as well as IL13Rα2 -tumor cells. By recapitulating the key aspects of brain TME cytoarchitecture, vascular barrier functionality, and by directly incorporating T cells adjacent to the tumor core, our GOC system effectively models locoregional T cell administration relevant to a clinical setting. Through our on-chip functional and molecular assays, such as 3D invasion, real-time CAR T-tumor interaction tracking, and cytokine profiling, we demonstrated the system's novel capability to evaluate the efficacy, specificity, and cytokine dynamics of CAR T cell therapy for GBM. Furthermore, the enhanced functional response of CAR T cells observed within this physiologically relevant environment provides novel insights unattainable with existing models, such as the ability to assess vascular damage as a safety measure and to enable quantitative analysis of target-to-T cell interactions. In conclusion, we developed an organotypic microfluidic GOC model that closely mimics tumor cytoarchitecture, offering a sophisticated, high-throughput, and costeffective platform for assessing CAR T cell efficacy against solid tumors.
